results.content: Three common methods for addressing the problem are (a) complete-case analysis, where only units that are complete on the variables in an analysis are included; (b) weighting, where the complete cases are weighted by the inverse of an estimate of the probability of being complete; and (c) multiple imputation (MI), where missing values of the variables in the analysis are imputed as draws from their predictive distribution under an implicit or explicit statistical model, the imputation process is repeated to create multiple filled-in data sets, and analysis is carried out results.title: Nonresponse Bias Analysis in Longitudinal Studies: A Comparative Review with an Application to the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study - Si - 2024 - International Statistical Review - Wiley Online Library
results.content: Our NRBA compares inferences for questions of interest based on alternative approaches to adjusting for nonresponse, where CCA includes different weighting methods and ACA includes weighting, multiple imputation (MI; Rubin, 1987), multilevel models with maximum likelihood (ML) estimation (e.g. Fitzmaurice *et al*., 2009), marginal models fitted by generalised estimating equations (GEEs; Liang & Zeger, 1986) and Bayesian modelling (Daniels & Hogan, 2008). Our paper differs from previous review articles (e.g. Ibrahim *et al*., 2005; Ibrahim & Molenberghs, 2009; Brick, 2013) by simultaneously handling unit, wave and item nonresponse in a longitudinal survey, attrition-adjusted weighting, extensive discussions of MI-related developments and proposed extensions of sensitivity analysis. * AC, available case; ACA, available case analysis; ACA-attr-w, attrition-adjusted, conditional on the baseline information, weighted analysis accounting for the cluster structure by individuals with available cases; ACA-base-w, base weighted analysis accounting for the cluster structure by individuals with available cases; ACA-seq-attr-w, attrition-adjusted, conditional on the previous information, weighted analysis accounting for the cluster structure by individuals with available cases; CC, complete case; CCA, complete case analysis; CCA-attr-w, attrition-adjusted weighted analysis accounting for the cluster structure by individuals with complete cases; CCA-base-w, base weighted analysis accounting for the cluster structure by individuals with complete cases; GEE, generalized estimating equation with a specified working correlation matrix; MAR, missing at random; MCAR, missing completely at random; MI, multiple imputation with sequential wave by wave conditional imputation; MI-offset, sensitivity analysis with an offset. We conduct sequential conditional MI to handle both unit and item nonresponse using *mice* (Van Buuren, 2012), tailoring the imputation models to the incomplete variable types: logistic regression models for binary variables (e.g. sex and school types), multinomial logistic regression models for nominal variables (e.g. race/ethnicity), ordinal logistic regression models for ordered variables (e.g. poverty levels and social-economic status), tree-based methods for non-normally distributed numeric variables (e.g. age and per cent of non-White students) and predictive mean matching for the assessment outcome (e.g. reading IRT scores). We compare weighting, MI, repeated-measures models that allow for missing data and sensitivity analysis approaches for NRBA in longitudinal studies. Our NRBA focuses on the monotone response pattern, fits regressions of key survey outcomes and indicators of nonresponse on variables observed for both respondents and nonrespondents, compares estimates with and without nonresponse weighting adjustments and implements sensitivity analyses based on adding offsets to MI results to assess the impact of deviations from MAR missingness.

results.title: Longitudinal Insights - Number Analytics
results.content: One of the most effective ways to conduct longitudinal research is through cohort surveys, which involve collecting data from the same group of participants at multiple points in time. This involves defining your research question and objectives, identifying your target cohort and sampling frame, and determining the survey frequency and duration. The following flowchart illustrates the key considerations when planning a cohort survey: Define Research Question and Objectives Identify Target Cohort and Sampling Frame Determine Survey Frequency and Duration Develop Survey Instrument and Data Collection Plan ### Data Collection and Management Once you have planned your cohort survey, it's time to collect and manage your data. Some strategies for recruiting participants include: * Using social media and online advertising to reach a wider audience * Partnering with organizations or businesses to access your target cohort * Using incentives or rewards to encourage participation Some strategies for retaining participants include: * Regular communication and updates on the study progress * Providing incentives or rewards for completing surveys * Using multiple channels to contact participants (e.g., email, phone, mail) #### Best Practices for Survey Administration and Data Collection To ensure high-quality data, it's essential to follow best practices for survey administration and data collection. Some methods for handling missing data include: * Listwise deletion: excluding participants with missing data from the analysis * Multiple imputation: imputing missing values using statistical models * Inverse probability weighting: weighting participants by the inverse probability of being missing Some methods for handling attrition include: * Using multiple imputation to impute missing data for participants who drop out * Using inverse probability weighting to weight participants by the inverse probability of dropping out * Analyzing the characteristics of participants who drop out to identify potential biases #### Interpreting Results and Drawing Meaningful Conclusions Interpreting the results of your cohort survey requires careful consideration of the study design, data quality, and statistical analysis. A: A cohort survey is a type of longitudinal study that involves collecting data from the same group of participants at multiple points in time. A: Yes, cohort surveys can be used to study rare outcomes, but you may need to use specialized statistical techniques, such as survival analysis, to analyze the data.
